questions.question: What is the difference between trivalent and hexavalent chromium in food?
questions.answer: Chromium in the food system is a split case between two species. Trivalent chromium (Cr3+) has an ambiguous history as a putative essential trace element and is the form found in most dietary supplements. Hexavalent chromium (Cr6+) is a carcinogen by inhalation and has documented toxicity by ingestion, including in drinking water, so the two species differ sharply and are tracked separately.

questions.question: How does hexavalent chromium get into food?
questions.answer: According to the page, hexavalent chromium's relevance to food is principally through drinking water used in food preparation, through meat processing with certain contact materials, and through supply-chain contamination. Because of these distinct pathways, Cr6+ is handled on its own dedicated page separate from trivalent chromium.

questions.question: What health effects are linked to hexavalent chromium exposure?
questions.answer: Drawing on [[sources/ufelle2021-metals-chapter|Ufelle & Barchowsky 2021]], hexavalent chromium is absorbed through sulfate and phosphate transporters and is associated with corrosive injury, allergic contact dermatitis, and acute renal injury after high-dose ingestion. That source also frames Cr(VI) in terms of lung cancer and genotoxicity. These effects are specific to the hexavalent species.

questions.question: Is trivalent chromium (the kind in supplements) considered safe or essential?
questions.answer: The page describes trivalent chromium as having an ambiguous history as a putative essential trace element, and notes it is the species present in most dietary supplements. It does not resolve the essentiality question; the page is a sourced stub and states that Cr-III-specific expansion, including the essentiality debate and supplement context, awaits dedicated corpus ingest.

questions.question: Why does it matter whether a study reports 'total chromium' instead of the specific species?
questions.answer: The wiki maintains the Cr3+ versus Cr6+ distinction wherever the source permits, and flags ambiguity when a study reports total chromium without specifying the species. Sources that report total chromium without speciating are treated only as total-chromium occurrence context and must not be silently substituted for hexavalent chromium, because Cr-VI's toxicology, occurrence, regulatory, and testing posture all differ sharply from Cr-III.
